items.q: Why do communication tips fail without mindset shifts?
items.a: It's like a chef who **keeps collecting recipes but never cooks**. Frameworks without mental models leave you trapped — six shifts cover nerves, rambling, dry topics, interviews, criticism, and practice.

items.q: How do you turn self-consciousness into useful focus?
items.a: Nerves burn capacity on **"me me me."** Become **audience-conscious**: focus on one person you might help — the American **"how can I serve you?"** frame. **"You're no longer self-conscious — you are now audience conscious."**
Open with **"the one thing"** to force end-in-mind focus. Escalate later to **"the two things"** or **"top three things"** when ready.

items.q: Can a boring industry still be engaging?
items.a: **Topic ≠ communicator.** Neil deGrasse Tyson makes physics lovable; boring professors make finance hated. Use **metaphors, demos, and funny visuals** — **"you don't have to be boring."**

items.q: How should you answer "tell me about yourself"?
items.a: Treat it as a **free story slot**, not an adjective résumé. Behavioral questions are hidden story prompts too — **rapport and storytelling beat raw intelligence** (Brad gets the job while smarter candidates list traits).

items.q: Whose feedback should you actually weight?
items.a: **Man in the Arena** — only people doing the work with you (Roosevelt via Brené Brown). Trying to **please everyone → please no one**; the spotlight effect means others fixate on their own butter, not your vocal slip.
**Every time you open your mouth** — that's composing. Solo self-talk counts. You don't **rise to the occasion**; you **fall back to your level of preparation**. Luck = preparation + opportunity.
